parole.significato: Used to form nouns denoting action, or a person performing said action.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish -ado, from Latin -āta, feminine form of -ātus, suffix used to create adjectives and nouns.

parole.significato: Counsel; advisor; counselor; barrister.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish abogado, from Latin advocātus, from advocō (“to call, summon”). Doublet of advocate.

parole.significato: A Latin American embrace.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish abrazar (“to embrace”), from a + brazo (“arm”), from Latin bracchium.

parole.significato: A Hispanic grandmother.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish abuela.

parole.significato: A Hispanic grandfather.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish abuelo.

parole.significato: Densely packed crushed rock covering the ground where a bullfight will take place.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish albero.

parole.significato: Either of two species of large amphibious reptile, Alligator mississippiensis or Alligator sinensis, in the genus Allig…
parole.testo: ] From early Modern English alligater, alligarta, aligarto, alegarto, alagarto, from Spanish el lagarto (“the lizard”), from Latin lacertus (“lizard”), modern spelling possibly influenced by the unrelated Latin alligator (“one who binds”).

parole.significato: A friend.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish amigo (“friend”), from Latin amīcus (“friend”), derived from amāre (“to love”). Compare French ami, Italian amico, Portuguese amigo and Romanian amic. Doublet of amicus.

parole.significato: A traditional Spanish unit of land area, equivalent to about 4472 m², chiefly used for vineyards and olive groves.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish aranzada, from aranzata (“ration”), from Old Spanish arenzo and arienço (“Spanish coin”), from Latin argenteus (“silvery, silver piece”).

parole.significato: A fleet of warships, especially with reference to the Spanish Armada.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish armada (“fleet, navy”), from Medieval Latin armāta, from the feminine past participle of Latin armō, from arma. Doublet of army.

parole.significato: A dry creek or streambed, a gulch which temporarily or seasonally fills and flows (after sufficient rain).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish arroyo.

parole.significato: Any of various dishes made from grilled or barbecued meat originating in Latin American and Philippine cuisine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish asado (“grilled”), from Latin assātus (“roasted”), past participle of Latin assō (“to roast, broil”), from assus (“roasted”) + -ō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eHs-. Partially borrowed from Tagalog asado from the same origin.

parole.significato: A contract or convention between Spain and other powers for providing African slaves for the Spanish colonies in Americ…
parole.testo: From Spanish asiento (“seat, contract or agreement”), from asentar (“to place on a chair, to adjust, to make an agreement”), from a- + sentar (“a participial verb”), from Latin ad + *sedentare (“to cause to sit”), from sedens, sedentis.

parole.significato: A stupid fellow, an ass.
parole.testo: From Spanish asnico, diminutive of asno, from Latin asinus, cognate with English ass (donkey).

parole.significato: A former currency of Argentina. Its symbol was ₳.
parole.testo: From Spanish austral, from Latin australis.

parole.significato: A historical stringed instrument similar in form to a guitar; a pandore.
parole.testo: From Spanish bandurria, from Latin pandura, pandurium, a musical instrument of three strings, from Ancient Greek πανδοῦρα (pandoûra, “three-stringed lute”). Compare pandore, banjo, mandolin, bandura.

parole.significato: A plant (Lonchocarpus urucu, now Deguelia rufescens var. urucu) native to parts of northern South America used as a poi…
parole.testo: From American Spanish barbasco, perhaps alteration of Spanish verbasco, varbasco (“mullein”), from Latin verbascum.

parole.significato: A storehouse for maturing wine, a winery.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish bodega, from Latin apothēca (“storehouse”), from Ancient Greek ἀποθήκη (apothḗkē, “storehouse”). Doublet of apotheke and boutique. In New York popularized by the Puerto Rican community.

parole.significato: A form of traditional drumming, and an associated form of dance, from Puerto Rico.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish bomba.

parole.significato: A rich mine or vein of silver or gold.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish bonanza (“dead calm, fair weather, good luck, rich lode”), from Vulgar Latin *bonacia (“lull, dead calm”), in turn from Latin malacia (“calm sea”), influenced by bonus (“good”) under the false impression that initial mal- is a derivate of malus (“bad”).

parole.significato: A stupid person.
parole.testo: 17th century. From Spanish bobo, from Latin balbus (“stammering”). (bird): Compare typologically Translingual Morus, German Tölpel, Polish głuptak (akin to głupek), Russian о́луша (óluša) (akin to о́лух (ólux)).

parole.significato: A drunkard.
parole.testo: From Spanish borracho (“drunkard, wine bottle”), from Latin burrus (“red, flushed”), from Ancient Greek πυρρός (purrhós, “tawny, red”).

parole.significato: A gallery forest found growing along a river bank or on the flood plain of a watercourse.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish bosque (“forest”), from Late Latin boscus, from Frankish *busc (compare Middle Dutch busch), from Proto-Germanic *buskaz (“forest, woods”); perhaps also influenced by bosk. The word is a doublet of bush.

parole.significato: Synonym of estado, a traditional Spanish unit of length equivalent to about 1.67 m.
parole.testo: From Spanish braza (“Spanish brace”), from Old Spanish braça, from Latin brachia, variant of bracchium (“arm, cubit”), from Ancient Greek βραχίων (brakhíōn, “upper arm”).

parole.significato: A bulb-shaped bud in the place of a flower or in a leaf axil.
parole.testo: From Spanish bulbillo, from the diminutive form of Latin bulbus, from Ancient Greek βολβός (bolbós, “plant with round swelling on underground stem”).

parole.significato: A Mexican dish consisting of a flour tortilla wrapped around a filling of meat and/or beans, cheese etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish burrito, diminutive of burro (“donkey”), from burrico (“donkey”), from Latin burricus (“small horse”), from burrus (“red-brown”), from Ancient Greek πυρρός (purrhós, “flame-colored”), from πῦρ (pûr, “fire”). A possible origin is due to its resemblance to a rolled up pack as typ

parole.significato: A small donkey, especially when used as a pack animal or one that is feral and lives in the southwestern United States…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish burro.

parole.significato: A medieval Spanish land tenure equivalent to a knight's fee, held under an obligation for military service.
parole.testo: From Spanish caballería, from caballero (“horseman, gentleman, cowboy”) + -ía (“-y: forming nouns”), from Late Latin caballārius (“horseman, rider”), from Latin caballus (“horse”) + -ārius (“-ary”). Doublet of cavalry and chivalry.

parole.significato: A horseman, particularly in the Latin American context
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish caballero. Doublet of cavalier and chevalier.

parole.significato: A horse.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish caballo (“horse”).

parole.significato: A local government council in some Spanish-speaking communities.
parole.testo: From Spanish cabildo, from Latin capitulum. Doublet of chapter, chapiter, capitule, and capitulum.

parole.significato: A burr gherkin.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish calabaza.

parole.significato: A glossy woolen fabric with striped or checkered designs.
parole.testo: From Spanish calamaco, from Late Latin calamaucus (“skullcap”).

parole.significato: A large crater formed by collapse of the cone or edifice of a volcano.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish caldera (“cauldron”), from Late Latin caldāria (“warm bath”), from Latin caldārium. Doublet of chowder.

parole.significato: A crude form of sodium nitrate from South America; used as a fertilizer.
parole.testo: From Spanish caliche, from Latin calx (“pebble”); compare chalk.

parole.significato: A tropical tree, Lucuma campechiana, from Central America and the Caribbean, that bears a sweet oval fruit.
parole.testo: From dialectal variant of Spanish canastillo (“small basket”), from Latin canistellum, diminutive of canistrum (“basket”).

parole.significato: Any of several large columnar cacti mostly of the genus Cereus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish cardón, from from Late Latin cardōnem, from Latin cardus, alternative form of carduus (“thistle”). Doublet of cardoon and chard.

parole.significato: A traditional Spanish unit of dry measure, equivalent to about 222 liters.
parole.testo: From Spanish carga (“a load, 4 Spanish bushels”), from cargar (“to load”), from Late Latin carricāre, from Latin carrus (“cart”). Doublet of charge and cargo.

parole.significato: Freight carried by a ship, aircraft, or motor vehicle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish cargo (“load, burden”), from cargar (“to load”), from Late Latin carricō. Doublet of charge and carga. Displaced native Old English fearm.

parole.significato: A single handheld percussion instrument consisting of a pair of concave shells or shell-shaped parts joined on one edge…
parole.testo: From Spanish castañeta, diminutive form of castaña, from Latin castanea, from Ancient Greek καστάνεια (kastáneia, “chestnut”), possibly of Pre-Greek origin. Related to the chest in chestnut, formerly chesten.

parole.significato: A traditional Spanish unit of mass, equivalent to about 4.8 g.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish castellano (“Castilian”), from Medieval Latin Castella (“Castile, Land of Fortresses”) + -ānus (“-an: forming adjectives”), from Latin castrum (“fort”) + -ella (“-elle: forming diminutives”). Doublet of Castilian, castellanus, castellan, and chatelain.

parole.significato: A leader.
parole.testo: From Spanish caudillo, from Late Latin capitellum, based on Latin caput, capitis (“head”). Doublet of caddie, cadel, cadet, capital, and capitellum. More possible, from kaput and ili (iri, ür, uri: town), from Basque language. In Iberian ili is high point, high city.

parole.significato: Synonym of ravine: a gully, a narrow (often small) canyon.
parole.testo: From Spanish cañada, from Latin canna (“cane”) + -ada (“-ed”).

parole.significato: Salted, dried meat.
parole.testo: From Spanish cecina, from Vulgar Latin *siccīna (“jerky”), from Latin siccus (“dry”).

parole.significato: A monetary unit worth one-hundredth of the main currency in Uruguay, Panama and (formerly) Chile.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish centésimo.

parole.significato: A Latin-American boy; a Latino.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish chico.

parole.significato: Cyperus esculentus, a species of sedge native to warm temperate to subtropical regions of the Northern Hemisphere havin…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish chufa, possibly from Latin cȳphi (“gallingale perfume”), from Ancient Greek κῦφι (kûphi, “a kind of Egyptian incense”), from Egyptian kꜣpt (“incense”), a nominal derivative of kꜣp (“to cense”).

parole.significato: The stems and leaves of the coriander plant, Coriandrum sativum, used as a seasoning and garnish in cooking.
parole.testo: From Spanish cilantro, possibly from an unattested regional Vulgar Latin variant (with a front vowel) of Late Latin coliandrum, from Latin coriandrum (“coriander”). Doublet of coriander and culantro.

parole.significato: A characteristic pattern of beats, especially the 3-2 son clave.
parole.testo: From Spanish clave, from Latin clāvis (“key”). Doublet of clavis and clef.

parole.significato: A percussion instrument, consisting of two sticks or blocks, in which one is struck against the other in order to produ…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin American Spanish claves (plural), from Latin clāvis (“a key; a lever, bar”).

parole.significato: A traditional Spanish unit of length, equivalent to about 41.6 cm.
parole.testo: From Spanish codo (“elbow, Spanish cubit”), from Old Spanish cobdo, from Latin cubitus, from cubitum (“elbow, Roman cubit”). Doublet of cubit and covado. Compare codo.

parole.significato: A silver ornament either stamped with a design or inlaid with a stone.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish concha (“shell”).

parole.significato: A member of the personal guard of the medieval and early modern Spanish or Portuguese kings.
parole.testo: From Spanish continuo, ellipsis of hombre continuo (“constant and steadfast man”), from Latin continuus (“constant, continuous”).

parole.significato: Dorstenia contrajerva, a South American plant whose aromatic root is sometimes used in medicine as a gentle stimulant a…
parole.testo: From Spanish contrayerba (“literally, a counter-herb, hence an antidote for poison”), from Latin contra + herba (“herb”).

parole.significato: Any of several small marine clams, of the species Donax variabilis, common in United States coastal waters.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish coquina (“cockle”), from Latin concha (“bivalve, mollusk; mussel”), from Ancient Greek κόγχη (kónkhē, “mussel; shell”). Related to conch and conk.

parole.significato: A traditional Spanish unit of length, equivalent to about 10.4 cm.
parole.testo: From Spanish coto (“half-span, quarter-cubit”), supposedly a variant of codo (“Spanish cubit”), from Vulgar Latin forms of Latin cubitum (“elbow, Roman cubit”), but more probably a development of or influenced by Latin quārtus (“a fourth”) from its use as a fourth of the cubit or Latin quattuor (“fo

parole.significato: A traditional Spanish unit of dry measure, equivalent to about 13.9 L.
parole.testo: From Spanish cuartilla, from cuarto and cuarta (“fourth, quarter”) + -illa (“-elle: forming diminutives”), from Latin quartus (“fourth”). Doublet of cuartillo and quartilho.

parole.significato: A traditional Castilian unit of dry measure, equivalent to about 1.2 L.
parole.testo: From Spanish cuartillo (“¹⁄₄₈ Castilian bushel, &c.”), from Old Spanish quartillo (“little fourth”) in reference to its forming a fourth celemin, from quarto + -illo (“-elle: forming diminutives”), from Latin quartus (“one-fourth”). Doublet of cuartilla and quartilho.

parole.significato: A traditional Spanish unit of dry measure, equivalent to about 27.8 L.
parole.testo: (unit of measure): From Spanish cuarto (“quarter-sack”), from Latin quartus (“fourth, quarter”). Doublet of quart, quarter, and cuarta, etc.

parole.significato: A 10-line verse or stanza, (chiefly) in the form of a song comprising an introductory verse followed by four such divis…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish décima, from Latin decima (“a tenth”). Doublet of decim, decime, and dime.

parole.significato: A topless female street performer covered in body paint who poses for photographs in exchange for tips in the pedestria…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish desnuda, the feminine singular of desnudo (“naked, nude, undressed”), ultimately from Latin nūdus (“naked, nude, undressed”) and Proto-Indo-European *negʷ- (“bare, naked”).

parole.significato: A bold outlaw, especially one from southern portions of the Wild West.
parole.testo: From obsolete Spanish desperado, past participle of desperar, archaic form of desesperar (“to despair”), from Latin disperare (“to despair, to lose hope”), from prefix dis- + sperare (“to hope”). Doublet of desperate.

parole.significato: The Devil or a devil.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish diablo (“devil”). Doublet of diabolo, devil, diable, and diabolus.

parole.significato: A medieval Iberian coin.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish dinero (“money”). Doublet of denar, denarius, denier, dinar, diner, and dinheiro.

parole.significato: sweetheart, ladylove
parole.testo: From Spanish Dulcinea, the name of Don Quixote's mistress in Cervantes' romance. The name in Spanish is derived from Latin dulce, from Latin dulcis.

parole.significato: An order by the government prohibiting ships from leaving port.
parole.testo: From Spanish embargar (“to arrest”), from late Latin *imbarricāre (“to bar”), from Latin in- + Vulgar Latin *barra (“bar, barrier”).

parole.significato: To enclose or suit (a person) in armour.
parole.testo: Possibly: * from em- (a variant of en- (prefix meaning ‘in, into’)) + boss (“(small) cask; leather bottle for holding wine”) (Scotland, obsolete); or * borrowed from Spanish embozarse, from embozar (“to cloak, hide; to turn up; to wrap up”) + se (“oneself; yourself; himself; herself; etc.”). Embozar

parole.significato: A traditional Spanish unit of mass, equivalent to about 1.2 g and chiefly used for medicines.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Spanish escrúpulo, from Latin scrūpulus (“scruple, nagging doubt, ¹⁄₂₄ uncia”), from scrūpus (“sharp stone, anxiety”) + -ulus (“-ule: forming diminutives”). Doublet of scruple and escropulo.

parole.significato: Either of two species of perennial grasses used for fibre production, and for making paper:
parole.testo: From Spanish esparto, via Latin spartum from Ancient Greek σπάρτον (spárton, “rope, cable; esparto or halfah grass”), valued for its high tensile strength, used for cords and wicker, and exported by Spanish Greek colonies throughout the Mediterranian.

parole.significato: yellow bells (Tecoma stans)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish esperanza (“hope”).

parole.significato: A traditional Spanish unit of length, equivalent to about 3.3 m.
parole.testo: From Spanish estadal, from estado + -al, from Latin stātus (“state, status, standing”). Doublet of state, status, and estado.

parole.significato: A traditional Spanish unit of length, equivalent to about 1.67 m.
parole.testo: From Spanish estado (“Spanish fathom, state, status”), from Latin stātus (“standing, state, status”). Doublet of state, status, estate, and stade.

parole.significato: A sword in pre-Roman Iberia having a concave edge to the blade.
parole.testo: From Spanish falcata, from Latin falcātus.

parole.significato: Money.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish feria.

parole.significato: A religious festival.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish fiesta, from Late Latin festa, from the plural of festum (“feast”). Doublet of feast, fest, and fete.

parole.significato: A type of artistic drawing and lettering, incorporating brightly coloured stylised lines, flowers and climbing plants,…
parole.testo: From Spanish fileteado, ultimately from Latin filum (“thread”), referring to fine painted lines.

parole.significato: A public prosecutor (UK) or a district attorney (US).
parole.testo: From Spanish fiscal, ultimately from Latin fiscus (“treasury”).

parole.significato: Various species of grass in the genus Bouteloua, including Bouteloua gracilis (blue grama)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish grama (“grass”), from Latin grāmina, plural of grāmen (“grass”).

parole.significato: A high-ranking nobleman in Spain or Portugal.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish grande (adjective), from Latin grandis (“large, great”). Doublet of grand and grande.

parole.significato: A traditional Spanish unit of mass, equivalent to about 50 mg.
parole.testo: From Spanish grano (“grain, 1/9216 Spanish pound”), from Latin grānus (“grain”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵr̥h₂nóm. Doublet of grain.

parole.significato: A beech tree, especially a Mexican beech (Fagus mexicana).

catena.termine: 􂀿materia􂁀 fāgea

parole.testo: From Spanish haya, from Old Spanish haya, from Latin [materia] fāgea (“hay wood”).

parole.significato: Spanish or Latin American ice cream.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish helado.

parole.significato: One of two traditional Spanish units of measure:
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish hemina, from Latin hēmīna, from Ancient Greek ἡμῑ́νᾱ (hēmī́nā).

parole.significato: A military peacekeeping association in medieval Spain.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish hermandad (“brotherhood”).

parole.significato: A man, a chap, a guy; especially a Hispanic or Spanish man.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish hombre (“man; human being”). Doublet of gome, homo, ombre, and omi.

parole.significato: A low, oven-shaped mound, common in volcanic regions, emitting smoke and vapours from its sides and summit.
parole.testo: Diminutive from Spanish horno (“oven”), from Latin furnus. See furnace.

parole.significato: An egg.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish huevo (“egg; testicle”). Doublet of egg, ey, oeuf, and ovum.

parole.significato: Fool or imbecile.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish idiota, from Latin idiōta (“idiot”), from Ancient Greek ἰδιώτης (idiṓtēs, “layman”) from ἴδιος (ídios, “private”). Doublet of idiot. By surface analysis, idi- + -ota.

parole.significato: a rebel, especially in Cuba or the Philippines during American military involvement there around the start of the 20th…
parole.testo: From Spanish insurrecto, from Latin īnsurrectus.

parole.significato: Any bird of the genus Junco, which includes several species of North American sparrow.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish junco (“reed, rush”), from Latin iuncus (“reed, rush”). Doublet of juncus and possibly junk.

parole.significato: The committee of military officers that have usurped political control.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish junta (literally "a thing gathered or joined"), feminine form of junto, from Latin iunctus, perfect passive participle of iungō (“join”). Attested from 1623.

parole.significato: A robber; a pirate; a rascal or rogue.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish ladrón, from Latin latrōnem, accusative singular of latrō. Doublet of latron.

parole.significato: A long rope with a sliding loop on one end, generally used in ranching to catch cattle and horses.
parole.testo: From Spanish lazo, from Vulgar Latin *laceum, from Latin laqueus. Doublet of lace.

parole.significato: The constellation of attributes common to many Latin American cultures and peoples.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish latinidad, from Latin Latīnitās. Doublet of Latinity.

parole.significato: A wolf.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish lobo (“wolf”). Doublet of lupus and wolf.

parole.significato: A Mexican professional wrestler, frequently (but not always) masked.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish luchador.

parole.significato: A sword-like tool used for cutting large plants with a chopping motion, or used as a weapon.
parole.testo: From Spanish machete, diminutive of macho (“sledgehammer”), from Latin mattea, possibly from mactare (“slaughter in sacrifice”); cognate with Old French machier, French massue, English mace.

parole.significato: Masculine in an overly assertive or aggressive way. Very masculine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish macho (“male”), from Latin masculus. Doublet of male.

parole.significato: An animal (usually an old mare), wearing a bell and acting as the leader of a troop of pack mules.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish madrina.

parole.significato: A high-quality grade of Spanish saffron.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish mancha (“stain”).

parole.significato: A tropical American tree (Hippomane mancinella), having apple-like, poisonous fruit, and a sap that causes blisters on…
parole.testo: From Spanish manzanillo, from manzana (“apple”), from Latin malum Matianum (“a kind of apple”).

parole.significato: A cocktail made with tequila, an orange-flavoured liqueur, and lemon or lime juice, often served with salt encrusted on…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish margarita. Doublet of Margaret (and various forms, q.v.), margarite, Margherita, and marguerite.

parole.significato: A type of siege engine similar to a trebuchet, designed to fling rocks over long distances.
parole.testo: See Spanish matar (“to kill”), Latin funda (“a sling”).

parole.significato: Tomorrow.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish mañana.

parole.significato: A traditional Spanish unit of dry measure, equivalent to about 2.3 L.
parole.testo: From Spanish medio (“half, half-celemin, half-real, etc.”), from Latin medius (“half”), from Proto-Italic *meðjos, from Proto-Indo-European *médʰyos (“between”). Doublet of medium, media, and mediate.

parole.significato: A kind of yellow-fleshed peach having red skin
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish melocotón (“peach tree and its fruit”), from Latin mālum cotōnium (“quince, or quince tree”, literally “apple of Cydonia”).

parole.significato: A flat area of land or plateau higher than other land, with one or more clifflike edges.
parole.testo: First attested 1759, from Spanish mesa (“table”), from Latin mēnsa. Doublet of mensa.

parole.significato: A person of mixed ancestry, especially one of Spanish and Native American heritage.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish mestizo, from Late Latin mixtīcius, from Latin mixtus (“mixed”). Doublet of metis, which came from French.

parole.significato: shit
parole.testo: Directly from Spanish mierda, from Latin merda. Doublet of merde and merd.

parole.significato: A traditional religious folk charm of Latin America and nearby regions, coming in a variety of forms.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish milagro (“miracle”), from Latin mīrāculum. Doublet of miracle and miraculum.

parole.significato: Spanish mile, a traditional Spanish unit of distance equivalent to about 1.4 km.
parole.testo: From Spanish milla (“Spanish mile”), from Latin mīlia (“Roman mile”), plural of mīlle (“1000”) in reference to its composition of 1000 Roman paces. Doublet of mile and milha.

parole.significato: A Cuban cocktail, generally made from rum, lime, sugar, mint, etc.
parole.testo: From Spanish mojito, diminutive of mojo (“sauce”), from mojar (“to moisten”), from Vulgar Latin *molliō (“to soften by soaking”), from Latin molliō (“soften”), from mollis (“soft”).

parole.significato: A small flying insect of the family Culicidae, the females of which bite humans and animals and suck blood, leaving an…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish mosquito (“gnat”), diminutive of mosca (“fly”), from Latin musca (“fly”), from Proto-Indo-European *mūs- (“fly, stinging fly, gnat”). Cognate with West Flemish meuzie (“mosquito”), dialectal Swedish mausa (“fly”), Lithuanian musė (“a fly”) and Sicilian muschitta (“midge”). See

parole.significato: Eucryphia cordifolia, a South American tree.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish muermo.

parole.significato: The loquat, Eriobotrya japonica.
parole.testo: From Spanish níspero (“medlar, loquat”), from Latin mespilum (“medlar”).

parole.significato: The ecclesiastic title of a permanent diplomatic representative of the Roman Catholic Church to a sovereign state or in…
parole.testo: From Spanish nuncio, from Latin nūntius (“envoy”).

parole.significato: The coypu, Myocastor coypus.
parole.testo: From Spanish nutria (“otter”), from Latin lutra.

parole.significato: A traditional Spanish unit of mass, equivalent to about 3.6 g.
parole.testo: From Spanish ochava (“⅛ Spanish ounce”), from Latin octāvus (“one-eighth”). Doublet of octave, octavo, and oitava.

parole.significato: A nitrate-producing factory in a Spanish-speaking country.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish oficina. Doublet of officina and usine.

parole.significato: A cooking-pot or earthenware jar used in Spain and Spanish-speaking countries.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish olla, from Latin ōlla, aulla; akin to Sanskrit उखा (ukhā, “pot”), and probably also Gothic 𐌰𐌿𐌷𐌽𐍃 (auhns, “oven”).

parole.significato: A traditional Spanish unit of mass, equivalent to about 28.76 g.
parole.testo: From Spanish onza (“ounce, Spanish ounce”), from Latin ū̆ncia. Doublet of a, one, inch, uncia, onça, oka, ouguiya, and awqiyyah.

parole.significato: A herb of the mint family, Origanum vulgare, having aromatic leaves.
parole.testo: 18th century, from Spanish orégano (“wild marjoram”), from Latin orīganum, from Ancient Greek ὀρίγανον (oríganon). Doublet of origanum.

parole.significato: A small family-run restaurant in a Cuban home
parole.testo: From Spanish paladar, from Old Spanish, from Vulgar Latin *palātārem, from Latin palātum.

parole.significato: Any of various fan palms of the family Arecaceae, especially Sabal palmetto or the saw palmetto, Serenoa repens.
parole.testo: From Spanish palmito, diminutive of palma (“palm tree”), from Latin palma. Doublet of palmite and palmito.

parole.significato: Synonym of cuarteron, a Spanish quarter-pound.
parole.testo: From Spanish panilla, from Latin panellus.

parole.significato: A treeless grassland ecosystem covering extensive high areas of equatorial mountains, especially in South America.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish páramo.

parole.significato: A small flaw or sin.
parole.testo: From Spanish pecadillo, diminutive form of pecado (“sin”), from Latin peccatum (“sin, error, fault”), from peccō (“to sin, offend”).

parole.significato: A short piece of chambered ordnance, used to fire stones in naval and siege warfare.
parole.testo: From Spanish pedrero, from Medieval Latin petrarium. Compare petrary.

parole.significato: A tall thin blade of hardened snow or ice, found closely spaced in large quantities at high altitudes.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish penitente, from the resemblance to white-hooded monks, from Latin paenĭtens, from paeniteō. Doublet of penitent.

parole.significato: Perfect, excellent, brilliant.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish perfecto (“perfect”), from Latin perfectus. Doublet of parfait, perfect, and perfectus.

parole.significato: A former unit of currency in Spain and Spain's colonies, worth 8 reales; the Spanish dollar.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish peso.

parole.significato: In the International System of Units and other metric systems of units, multiplying the unit to which it is attached by…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish pico (“beak, little bit, speck”)

parole.significato: Synonym of pimento, a cultivar of Capsicum annuum.
parole.testo: From Spanish pimiento (“bell pepper; later any pepper”), from Latin pigmentum (“coloring; colorful thing”), from pingō (“to paint”) and -mentum (suffix denoting instruments and results of actions). Doublet of pigment, piment, and pimento.

parole.significato: A plant in the genus Musa, the genus that includes banana, but with lower sugar content than banana.
parole.testo: From Spanish plantano (obsolete variant of plátano), from Latin platanus, from Ancient Greek πλάτανος (plátanos).

parole.significato: A town's public square.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish plaza (“town-square or central place of gathering”), from Latin platea, from Ancient Greek πλατεῖα (plateîa), clipping of πλατεῖα ὁδός (plateîa hodós, “broad way”). Doublet of piatza, piazza, place, and platz.

parole.significato: A town center, or the barangay where one is located.
parole.testo: From Spanish población, from Late Latin populātiō, populātiōnis, from Latin populus (“people”). Doublet of population.

parole.significato: A Central American fiesta costume usually heavily embroidered and very full in the skirt.
parole.testo: American Spanish pollera (“baby walker; chicken coop”) from pollo (“chicken”), from Latin pullus, pullō, from Proto-Indo-European *polH- (“animal young”).

parole.significato: A garrisoned place, especially one that is or was once under Spanish control.
parole.testo: From Spanish presidio (“garrison”), from Latin praesidium, 1763. Doublet of praesidium and presidium.

parole.significato: A card game resembling poker, dating back at least to the 16th century.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish primera, feminine form of primero (“first”), from Latin prīmārius. See premier.

parole.significato: A trusted friend; a confidant.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish privado, from Latin privatus.

parole.significato: Quickly, very soon, promptly.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish pronto, from Latin prōmptus. Doublet of prompt.

parole.significato: A community in Spain or Spanish America, especially one of Pueblo Indians living in a stone or adobe multi-storey build…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish pueblo, from Latin populus. Doublet of people.

parole.significato: A traditional Spanish unit of length, equivalent to about 2.3 cm
parole.testo: From Spanish pulgada, from Vulgar Latin *pollicata, from Latin pollicaris (“of or related to a thumb”), from pollex (“thumb”) + -āris (“-ary: forming adjectives”). Doublet of polegada.

parole.significato: A prostitute, whore, slut, bitch, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish puta.

parole.significato: A person considered three-fourths white, having one non-white grandparent.
parole.testo: From Spanish cuarterón (“¾ white, a child of a European and a mestizo”), from cuarto (“one-fourth”) + -on (“-oon: forming related nouns”), from Latin quartus (“one-fourth”). Doublet of cuarteron.

parole.significato: Warehouse receipt issued for stored commodities, especially sugar.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish quedan, ellipsis of quedan [depositadas] (“there are hereby deposited”), a phrase that appeared on the receipt. The term quedan is the third-person plural present indicative of quedar (“to remain”), from Old Spanish quedar, from Vulgar Latin *quētāre, from Late Latin quiētō, fr

parole.significato: A West Indian tree related to the mulberry , Trophis racemosa.
parole.testo: From Spanish [Term?], from Latin ramus (“branch”).

parole.significato: Former unit of currency of Spain and Spain's colonies.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish real (“royal”), from Latin rēgālis (“regal, royal”). Doublet of ariary, regal, riyal, and royal.

parole.significato: A monk of a reformed order.
parole.testo: From Spanish reformar, from Latin refōrmāre.

parole.significato: An outlaw or rebel.
parole.testo: From Spanish renegado, from Medieval Latin renegātus, perfect participle of renegō (“to deny”). See also renege.

parole.significato: A long quirt attached to the end of a set of closed reins that are connected to the bridle of a horse, and used to assi…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish ramal, from Latin ramus (“branch”).

parole.significato: A kind of salsa round dance.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish rueda.

parole.significato: A traditional Spanish unit of dry measure, equivalent to about 111 L.
parole.testo: From Spanish saco (“a sack, a half-carga”), from Old Spanish saco, from Latin saccus, from Ancient Greek σάκκος (sákkos, “sack, sackcloth”), from Semitic. Doublet of sac, saccus, sack, and sakkos.

parole.significato: A spicy tomato sauce of Mexican origin, often including onions and hot peppers.
parole.testo: PIE word  *sḗh₂l Borrowed from Spanish salsa (“sauce”), from Latin salsus (“salted”), whence also the doublet sauce (via Old French).

parole.significato: A tray used to display or serve food or other items (such as a visiting card).
parole.testo: From Middle English salver (“serving platter”), from Spanish salva (“a testing of food or drink to test for poison”), from salvar (“to save, taste food for one's master”), from Latin salvō (“save”, verb). More at save.

parole.significato: A wooden or ivory statue of a saint, angel or other religious figure, found in Spain and former Spanish colonies.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish santo.

parole.significato: A tree of species Sassafras albidum of the eastern United States and Asia having mitten-shaped leaves and red, aromatic…
parole.testo: From Spanish sasafrás, possibly from Latin saxifragus (“stone-breaking”) from the habit of certain plants growing in cracks in boulders. If this etymology is correct, it is a doublet of saxifrage.

parole.significato: A traditional Spanish unit of length, equivalent to about 13.9 cm.
parole.testo: From Spanish sesma, from Latin sexta (“sixth”), from its use as a sixth of the vara (Spanish yard or rod).

parole.significato: A nap, especially an afternoon one taken during the hottest part of the day in some cultures.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish siesta, from Latin sexta (“the sixth hour from dawn, noon, midday”). Doublet of sext.

parole.significato: A former Spanish-American silver coin.
parole.testo: PIE word  *sóh₂wl̥ From Spanish sol (“sun”), from Latin sōl (“sun”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sóh₂wl̥ (“sun”). Doublet of Sol and sol, directly from the Latin.

parole.significato: A unit of length notionally based on the height of a grown man, equivalent to a fathom.
parole.testo: From Spanish estado, from Latin status (“standing”), in reference to it being roughly the height of a grown man. Doublet of estate, state, status, and estado.

parole.significato: A dockworker involved in loading and unloading cargo, or in supervising such work.
parole.testo: From Spanish estibador (cognate with Portuguese estivador, and compare Medieval Latin stivator), from estivar, estibar (“to load”), from Medieval Latin stivare, stīpāre (compare Italian stivare, stipare), the present active infinitive of stīpō (“to cram, fill, stuff”), derived from Proto-Indo-Europe

parole.significato: A tavern in Spain.
parole.testo: From Spanish taberna, from Latin taberna. Doublet of tavern and taverna.

parole.significato: A sloth (animal).
parole.testo: From Spanish tardo (“slow”), from Latin tardus.

parole.significato: A kind of red wine of a deep red color, chiefly from Galicia or Malaga in Spain.
parole.testo: From Spanish tinto (“deep-colored”), from Latin tīnctus, past participle of tingo (“to dye”). More at tinge. Doublet of tint and tinto. Compare claret (“French red wine”), also from color.

parole.significato: Any of the three stages of a bullfight: the vara, the banderilla and finally the death.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish tercio.

parole.significato: A bullfighter, especially one on horseback.
parole.testo: From Spanish toreador, from torear (“to fight bulls”), from toro (“bull”), from Latin taurus.

parole.significato: A violent wind in the form of a mobile, rapidly rotating, funnel cloud that has contacted the ground.
parole.testo: From earlier English ternado, attested since the 1550s as a nautical term for a windy thunderstorm. From Spanish tronada (“thunderstorm”), from tronar (“to thunder”), from Latin tonō (“to thunder”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tenh₂- (“to thunder”). The o and r were reversed in English (metathesis)

parole.significato: A sandwich, served either hot or cold, on an oblong white sandwich roll, derived from Mexican cuisine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish torta, from Latin turta, thought to derive from Latin tŏrta f (“twisted”). Doublet of torte and tart.

parole.significato: A Spanish form of nougat made from almonds and honey.
parole.testo: From Spanish turrón, probably from Latin torrere (“to roast”).

parole.significato: A kind of sweet orange.
parole.testo: From Spanish Valencia, from Latin Valentia, from valentia (“power, vigour”). Doublet of Valence.

parole.significato: A wand or staff of authority or justice.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish vara (“staff, wand”), Latin vara (“forked pole”).

parole.significato: A member of a vigilance committee.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish vigilante (“watchman, guard”), from Latin vigilans. Doublet of vigilant.

parole.significato: A traditional Spanish (or Portuguese) folk song with short stanzas and a refrain; now especially common as a Christmas…
parole.testo: From Spanish villancico, from villano (“peasant”), from Medieval Latin vīllānus (“villager”).

parole.significato: A traditional Spanish unit of land area, equivalent to about 32.2 hectares.
parole.testo: From Spanish yugada, from yugo (“yoke”) + -ada (“-ful”), from Latin iugum. Compare Latin iugerum (“juger”).
